definition: Categorical means absolute and without exceptions — said of statements, denials, and rules.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word categorical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know categorical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The chef's ban on shortcuts is categorical: no bottled dressing, no frozen dough, and no exceptions on busy nights.
Firm is milder than categorical — a firm no can still soften under enough pressure, the way a categorical one never does.
Unwavering comes close but stops short of categorical — an unwavering stance holds steady over time, while a categorical refusal also rules out every exception in advance.

Unconditional means offered with no conditions attached — nothing the receiver must first do or keep doing — and it is said of support, surrender, and love. Categorical belongs instead to statements: a categorical denial or ban admits no exceptions. Gifts and backing are unconditional; denials and rules are categorical.

Outright means complete and total — an outright lie, an outright ban, an outright victory — stressing that the thing is fully itself, nothing partial about it. Categorical adds the idea of no exceptions even in principle: a categorical denial closes every door at once, future cases included.

Categorical means absolute — admitting no exceptions, no conditions, no 'unless.' A categorical refusal doesn't say 'probably not' or 'not this time'; it closes every door at once, which is why the word attaches so naturally to denials, bans, and guarantees.
Categorical is the formal word for absolute statements: a categorical denial, ban, or guarantee.

In speech, plain 'flat' or 'absolute' often serves — but when you want to stress that no exception exists even in principle, categorical says exactly that, which is why lawyers and press offices love it.
